bastard_reason: Weasels will ambush small mammals in their burrows, kill them, and then have a snooze, lining the burrow with the victim’s fur to keep warm.
not_bastard_reason: Weasel mums teach their baby kits to hunt within a few weeks of birth, making sure they can fend for themselves as quickly as possible.

bastard_reason: Robins peck at each other’s necks when fighting to try to sever their rivals’ spinal cords
not_bastard_reason: Robins have strong parental instincts and will even feed baby birds from completely different species

bastard_reason: Prairie dogs kill baby ground squirrels so that they don't grow up and compete for food
not_bastard_reason: Prairie dogs aerate and fertilise the soil, encouraging plants to grow and increasing biodiversity

bastard_reason: Flamingos are more likely to pick fights with “left-handed” birds, which curve their necks to the left, because they’re different
not_bastard_reason: Flamingos help their chicks to hatch by gently removing pieces of shell as they hatch

bastard_reason: Desert tortoises flip each other over in fights. If they can't flip back the right way, they get cooked in their shell by the sun or die of collapsed lungs
not_bastard_reason: Desert tortoises dig burrows to escape forest fires and share them with other creatures that otherwise might not survive

bastard_reason: Clownfish act as live bait for sea anemones to lure unsuspecting fish into the anemone's stinging tentacles
not_bastard_reason: Clownfish take good care of their sea anemone homes, removing parasites and fanning the anemone to make sure it gets enough oxygen

bastard_reason: King cobras have hyperalgesic proteins in their venom, which increase the amount of pain their prey feels before it dies
not_bastard_reason: King cobras are the only snakes to build nests, and go without food for several months while protecting their eggs

bastard_reason: Male wolf spiders eat old females because they have low reproductive potential so are considered more valuable as a snack than as a potential mother
not_bastard_reason: Wolf spiders have violin-like palps on their heads that they use to softly serenade potential mates

bastard_reason: Dominant ostriches force low-ranking females to lay eggs at the edge of a large shared nest, where they are more likely to be snatched by predators
not_bastard_reason: Ostriches use their large wings as chick parasols to shelter the baby birds from up to 50°C heat
picture_attribution: By William Warby - Flickr, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=17199030

bastard_reason: Spotted hyenas make false alarm calls when they find meals, scaring away others to avoid sharing food
not_bastard_reason: Spotted hyenas teach younger members of their group how to solve problems
picture_attribution: By [2] - [1], CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=45527715

bastard_reason: Zebras can be so hostile to new group members that the stallion has to protect new arrivals until they’re accepted by the herd
not_bastard_reason: Zebras stand nose to tail with their close friends, using their tails to flick flies off each other and watching each other’s back for predators
picture_attribution: By Muhammad Mahdi Karim - Own work, GFDL 1.2, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=10729821

bastard_reason: Ring-tailed lemurs cover their tails in smelly secretions, thrusting them like lances in "stink battles" where the smelliest lemur wins
not_bastard_reason: Ring-tailed lemurs keep their tails raised like flags when they’re on the move to make sure the group can stay together
picture_attribution: By Alex Dunkel (Maky) - Own work, CC BY 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=8621909

bastard_reason: If sun parakeets get hungry for calcium, they break and eat their own eggs
not_bastard_reason: If a sun parakeet is separated from the flock, it just has to squawk and the group will come back to fetch it
picture_attribution: By Brian Gratwicke - originally posted to Flickr as Sun Conure Aratinga solstitialis, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=8937472

bastard_reason: Squids cover their eggs in a special pheromone that makes fights break out among males, so the toughest ones end up fertilising the eggs
not_bastard_reason: Squids remove scientific equipment from each other to make swimming easier
picture_attribution: By Miguel Cabanellas (Mediterranean Institute for Advanced Studies) - BMC Ecology image competition: the winning images. BMC Ecology 2013, 13:6 doi:10.1186/1472-6785-13-6, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=37319912

bastard_reason: Anteaters fight by swatting at each other with their large claws, and sitting on or even riding their opponents
not_bastard_reason: During a drought, anteaters use their big claws to dig out water holes and let other forest animals drink and bathe with them
picture_attribution: By Malene Thyssen - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=94801

bastard_reason: Jays not only attack other birds, but mimic the sounds their victims make while they do it
not_bastard_reason: Male jays learn which food their partners like and make sure to bring their favourites during courtship
picture_attribution: By I, Luc Viatour, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=5933620

bastard_reason: Capybaras use their enormous buck teeth to bite their rivals' faces in fights
not_bastard_reason: Capybaras are super chill and let other animals sit on top of them, apparently without expecting anything in return
picture_attribution: By Charlesjsharp - Own work, from Sharp Photography, sharpphotography, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=44254293

bastard_reason: Cormorants don't leave the nest to poo and eventually their droppings kill the tree they're nesting in
not_bastard_reason: Cormorants help each other find fish and work together to make sure each bird catches more fish than they would alone
picture_attribution: By JJ Harrison (jjharrison89@facebook.com) - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=9761097

bastard_reason: Bald eagles steal food from other birds, aggressively attacking and even forcing their victims to throw up food they've already swallowed
not_bastard_reason: Most bird species let the weakest chicks die, but bald eagles feed smaller chicks first and stop fights in the nest
picture_attribution: By Saffron Blaze - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=18433764

bastard_reason: Great bustards eat little blister beetles, which don't provide any nutrition, but increase their sexual arousal
not_bastard_reason: Great bustards honour their elders. Older males have fewer fights because the younger males respect them
picture_attribution: By Andrej Chudý from Slovakia - Drop fúzatý (Otis tarda), CC BY-SA 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=39987827

bastard_reason: Kelp gulls strip the skin off whales’ backs when they come to the surface to breathe, especially targeting baby whales, which can’t shake them off as easily
not_bastard_reason: Kelp gulls protect their nest with vigour, dive-bombing much larger birds to drive them away
picture_attribution: By No machine-readable author provided. Gvasquez assumed (based on copyright claims). - No machine-readable source provided. Own work assumed (based on copyright claims)., CC BY-SA 2.5, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=607379

bastard_reason: Up to two dozen male humpbacks will fight over a single female, ramming each other and even holding other males underwater to drown them
not_bastard_reason: Humpbacks save members of completely different species from killer whales. One whale placed a seal on its own belly to keep it safe
picture_attribution: U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration

bastard_reason: Cuttlefish change colour to trick love rivals – males display to attract females on one half of their body, but pretend to be females on the other side so that other males ignore them
not_bastard_reason: If a male cuttlefish doesn't want to fight, he just turns pale. Other males then let him swim away in peace

bastard_reason: Moray eels prefer to prey on weak and dying animals, because they are easier to find and kill
not_bastard_reason: Moray eels look vicious because of the menacing way they open and close their mouths, but they're only taking in water to breathe, you judgemental bastard.

bastard_reason: Peacocks make fake mating noises to convince females that they are more sexually active than they really are
not_bastard_reason: Peahens work together to look after their babies and raise all the peachicks in a group

bastard_reason: Snails fire “love darts” before mating, sometimes lodging them in their partners’ internal organs or piercing them completely
not_bastard_reason: Marine snails carry their eggs on their backs to avoid them getting too hot or drying out on rocks

bastard_reason: Male newts pretend to be female to lure other males away from their displaying grounds. Then they steal the best spots to attract real females
not_bastard_reason: Newts wrap their eggs in leaves like little presents to protect them from predators and pollution

bastard_reason: Crocodiles balance twigs on their noses then hide underwater. When birds try to collect the nesting material, the crocodiles eat them
not_bastard_reason: Mother crocs will guard their eggs for months without moving or eating, and look after their offspring for years

bastard_reason: If threatened, sea cucumbers eject long sticky tubes from their anus to entangle whatever is bothering them
not_bastard_reason: Sea cucumbers protect their eggs in a special pouch, keeping them safe from predators while they develop
picture_attribution: By n (n) [Public domain], via Wikimedia Commons

bastard_reason: Coots kill ducklings and other baby birds, even their own offspring if food is scarce
not_bastard_reason: Coots warn each other of danger by dancing when they see a hawk or other predator

bastard_reason: Rabbits keep other rabbits out of their territory by doing extra-smelly poos using a gland in their anus to add secretions to each pellet
not_bastard_reason: Rabbits hum to their favourite friends and will "binky" when happy -- running, jumping and flicking their feet in joy

bastard_reason: Males can be very...enthusiastic...and try to mate with inanimate objects and even unwilling fish
not_bastard_reason: Toads avoid fighting and usually settle arguments by talking - based on how low they croak

bastard_reason: Lions prefer to scavenge rather than hunt and are much more likely to steal food from hyenas than vice versa
not_bastard_reason: Lionesses share parenting duties and babysit, protect, and even suckle each other's cubs

bastard_reason: Bowerbirds will secure the best food for themselves by knocking each other out of fruit trees
not_bastard_reason: If a male senses he is making a female uncomfortable, he will tone down the intensity of his courtship dance

bastard_reason: Wombats kill any intruders trying to enter their burrow by crushing the animal’s skull between their rear end and the roof of the burrow
not_bastard_reason: Wombat babies leave their mother's pouch after eight months, but their mothers will let them back inside if they get frightened
picture_attribution: By JJ Harrison (jjharrison89@facebook.com) - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=8661812

bastard_reason: If a flounder finds a clam too big to eat, it will eat the siphon – the clam’s only way of eating and breathing – and leave the rest to die
not_bastard_reason: Female flounders choose a partner based on how much time he spends courting them, and remain faithful even if bigger, stronger males are around
picture_attribution: By Tiit Hunt (Own work) [CC BY-SA 3.0 (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0)], via Wikimedia Commons

bastard_reason: Male sleepy lizards use their jaws to grab females by the head when mating, leaving them with visible wounds
not_bastard_reason: Sleepy lizards pair for life. If one is killed on the road, the other will stay with the body, nudging it gently to try and revive it
picture_attribution: By Alain Steffes (Own work) [CC BY-SA 2.5 (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.5)], via Wikimedia Commons

bastard_reason: Tarantula hawk moth larvae live inside spiders that have been paralysed by adults. The larvae avoid eating the spiders’ vital organs to keep them alive for as long as possible as they eat them
not_bastard_reason: Adult tarantula hawk wasps eat only nectar and fermented fruit, which gets them drunk

bastard_reason: Spadefoot toad tadpoles that eat shrimp early in life become entirely carnivorous, growing sharp teeth and eating other tadpoles
not_bastard_reason: Startled spadefoot toads produce skin secretions that smell like peanut butter
picture_attribution: By Sarah Beckwith [Public domain], via Wikimedia Commons

bastard_reason: Water voles catch frogs, eat just their legs and throw away the rest of the meat
not_bastard_reason: Water voles keep their burrows clean by devoting individual rooms to different kinds of food and having a separate toilet room
picture_attribution: © David Pérez (DPC), Wikimedia Commons, License cc-by-sa-4.0

bastard_reason: Wildebeest take out their frustration by beating trees with their horns, stripping bark and branches until the tree dies
not_bastard_reason: Wildebeest take turns sleeping to keep an eye out for predators, protecting their herd and any other prey animals around them
picture_attribution: By Muhammad Mahdi Karim (Own work) [GFDL 1.2 (http://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/fdl-1.2.html)], via Wikimedia Commons

bastard_reason: Dominant female meerkats don’t like to share attention so kick out low-ranking pregnant females from the group
not_bastard_reason: Meerkats will risk their own lives to protect pups, even if they're not related

bastard_reason: Seahorses save energy by using sea urchins as unwilling taxis
not_bastard_reason: Seahorse males incubate their eggs before they hatch, reducing the stress on females

bastard_reason: Dolphins have been documented masturbating with live eels
not_bastard_reason: Dolphins will stay with ill or injured dolphins and help them up to the surface to breathe

bastard_reason: Dung beetles will eat the eggs of other beetles so they can lay their own eggs in the best dung
not_bastard_reason: Male and female dung beetles work hard to dig nests to provide the best environment for their young

bastard_reason: Rats have a strict social hierarchy. If food or living space gets scarce, they kill the lowest-order members
not_bastard_reason: Rats giggle if you tickle their feet

bastard_reason: Tree kangaroos kill birds just to eat their brains, and throw the rest of the meat away
not_bastard_reason: Tree kangaroos play-fight with each other and play with falling leaves

bastard_reason: Great tits raid the food stores of smaller birds
not_bastard_reason: Great tits take time to prepare food for their chicks to make it easier to digest

bastard_reason: Vampire bats pretend to be chicks in order to snuggle with a mother hen, then slice her open and drink her blood
not_bastard_reason: Vampire bats check in with each other when they get back to roost and share food with bats who failed to find a blood meal

bastard_reason: Sea otters have been documented raping baby seals
not_bastard_reason: Sea otters hold hands while sleeping so they don't drift apart
